Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Priya Raman (Redwood CSM); Dr. Sara Patel (NimbusHealth ML Lead), James Liu (NimbusHealth SRE), Anoop Varma (NimbusHealth Product), Lina Gomez (NimbusHealth Data Eng)
summary: Weekly POC sync focused on cost/unit economics. Reviewed latest benchmark snapshots (tokens/sec and latency), discussed caching savings and batching tradeoffs. SE explained how Redwood's prefix/KV caching and batching windows change effective tokens per dollar and p95 latency. NimbusHealth raised concerns about tail latency for interactive workflows and asked for a 24h peak benchmark and an updated cost model. Identified action items: run extended benchmarks, share prompt corpus, and produce pricing scenarios for caching and batching configurations.
topics: Benchmark results review: tokens/sec/$, p50/p95 latencies
Cost model scenarios and estimate for production

transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, quick roll call. Maya from Redwood here, Luis and Priya on our side.
[00:06] Dr. Sara Patel: Hi all, Sara here.
[00:08] James Liu: James on the call.
[00:10] Anoop Varma: Anoop, product. Lina here too.
[00:14] Maya Chen: Great. Today we wanted to focus on the cost per unit economics you asked about - tokens per dollar, caching savings, and batching tradeoffs. Luis will walk through the numbers we ran last week.
[00:25] Luis Ortega: Cool, thanks Maya. So quick reminder of the test setup: hosted Redwood model rdx-13B-v1, 2k average request length, some requests have 6-8k prefix reuse. We ran mixes simulating your production distribution - morning peak and off-peak.
[00:43] Dr. Sara Patel: Quick Q - when you say prefix reuse, that's the KV cache you're referring to?
[00:48] Luis Ortega: Yeah, KV cache / prefix caching, same idea. We instrumented hits vs misses.
[00:52] Lina Gomez: FYI some of our chat flows have a repeated patient-history block that is about 850 tokens, that's the heavy prefix.
[00:58] Luis Ortega: Right - that showed up in the telemetry as high cache hit ratio for those flows.
[01:03] Luis Ortega: So headline numbers: with no caching and no batching baseline, effective tokens-per-dollar was about 95k tokens per $1 for the hosted config we used. When we enabled prefix caching only (TTL 10m) we saw average token consumption drop by ~34% for your prompt set, which improved tokens-per-dollar to ~145k/$1 - so roughly a 52% improvement in cost-efficiency compared to baseline.
[01:36] James Liu: Wait 34% saved tokens, and that maps to 52% better tokens per dollar? How's that math?
[01:42] Luis Ortega: Good catch - the reason it's >34% is because caching also reduces compute overhead by reducing KV operations and short-circuiting some decode steps; plus our billing has a small per-request overhead, so the relative improvement compounds.
[01:54] Dr. Sara Patel: That's promising. What about batching? We are very sensitive to latency - clinical use cases need snappy responses.
[02:00] Luis Ortega: Yes - so we tested three batching windows: no batching, 50ms, and 200ms. With 50ms window, tokens/sec throughput increased ~2.8x versus no batching, and cost per token dropped proportionally. However p95 latency went up from ~180ms to ~320ms in the 50ms case. With 200ms batching we got 4.6x throughput but p95 jumped to ~520ms, which is likely too high for interactive clinical workflows.
[02:31] Anoop Varma: So 50ms gives a 2.8x throughput increase but p95 320ms - that may be borderline for the UI. Can batching be adaptive? Like only batch for low-priority background tasks?
[02:40] Luis Ortega: Absolutely - you can route interactive routes with a low-latency policy that disables batching, and route background scoring/inference to a high-throughput policy that uses 200ms windows. This is a common hybrid strategy.
[02:51] Dr. Sara Patel: Do you have numbers that combine caching and batching? That's the realistic scenario for us.
[02:57] Luis Ortega: Yes - caching + 50ms batching for your prompt set produced effective tokens-per-dollar around 370k tokens per $1 - so combined wins are multiplicative. But latency p95 was around 340ms in that combined case; p50 stayed low (~120ms).
[03:15] Maya Chen: Important note: these numbers are from our hosted env and the model variant used. Performance will differ on dedicated or private due to hardware and kernel selection. We'll include that in the cost model.
[03:26] James Liu: Also curious about tail latency. Our SREs care about p99.
[03:29] Luis Ortega: p99 did increase - in the combined case p99 was ~720ms. We think that's driven by stragglers in the batch formation and some cold-start paths. We can address with admission controls and buster workers for small requests.
[03:45] Lina Gomez: Is there any way to throttle big prefixes? Some requests have 8k of static context which costs a lot every time.
[03:51] Luis Ortega: That's where prefix caching shines - if the 8k block is identical across sessions we cache KV for that prefix and then the marginal decode per request is much cheaper. For partially overlapping prefixes we can use fuzzy-cache heuristics but hit ratios drop.
[04:06] Dr. Sara Patel: Can we get an estimate of monthly spend at our projected 200k requests/day?
[04:11] Maya Chen: We did a rough calc in the spreadsheet - baseline (no cache, no batching) estimated to be about $32k/month. With caching + 50ms batching that drops to around $9k/month. We'll send the line-item spreadsheet after the call.
[04:23] Anoop Varma: That delta is huge - we need to validate with a longer run.
[04:26] Luis Ortega: Agreed - as action item we'll run a 24-hour benchmark during your peak window to validate the model against real timing and concurrency patterns. We'll provide tokens/sec, p50/p95/p99, and cost burn estimates.
[04:38] James Liu: One more thing on security: if we do prefix caching, where does the cache live? Is that customer-data-safe?
[04:45] Maya Chen: Good question. On hosted we encrypt at rest and access is restricted; for regulated data we recommend Private/VPC deployment so cache lives in your VPC and keys are customer-managed via KMS/HSM. We'll include security docs.
[04:58] Dr. Sara Patel: How about quantization? Could we use an int8 variant to save cost?
[05:02] Luis Ortega: Yes, quantized models can drop cost further, often 20-40% lower cost per token, but you have to evaluate quality for clinical language. For now we left quantization off in the baseline; we can add a QA sweep.
[05:16] Maya Chen: OK let's go through the concrete asks - Luis, are you comfortable to run the 24h peak test and share the harness link?
[05:22] Luis Ortega: Yep - I'll spin that up. I plan to run batch windows 1/50ms/200ms and caching TTLs 0/10m/60m, capture histograms.
[05:31] Lina Gomez: We'll upload sample prompt corpus to the S3 link Maya shared last week. Expect that today.
[05:36] Dr. Sara Patel: Also can you include a scenario for dedicated GPUs? We have a thread about bringing this to our infra team.
[05:41] Maya Chen: We'll add a dedicated scenario in the cost model - differences will be highlighted (e.g., kernel perf, amortized GPU cost).
[05:47] Anoop Varma: Any blockers on storage or data residency?
[05:50] Priya Raman: For Private we can support regional deployments and customer KMS; we'll follow up with security whitepaper and SOC2 docs.
[05:59] James Liu: Great.
[06:00] Luis Ortega: Quick note on numbers: some transcription from our instrumentation sometimes tags model names slightly differently - rdx-13B might show as rdx13b in logs. Just FYI for matching.
[06:12] Dr. Sara Patel: Understood.
[06:14] Maya Chen: Alright next: pricing sheet and benchmark harness link. I'll send both by tomorrow EOD.
[06:20] Dr. Sara Patel: Thanks.
[06:22] Anoop Varma: Thanks all.
[06:24] Maya Chen: We'll reconvene after the 24h run.
[06:27] James Liu: Sounds good.
[06:29] Lina Gomez: Bye.
[06:30] [meeting ends]

Notes on fidelity: transcription cleaned slightly for readability; occasional mis-hearings remain (e.g., 'K V cache' spaced). References: benchmark spreadsheet (link shared in chat), S3 prompt corpus link (provided), security whitepaper (will be attached).
